text:
Marcovitz c. Bruker

2005 QCCA 835

COURT OF APPEAL

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

REGISTRY OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-09-013353-032

(500-05-009878-891)

CORAM:

THE HONOURABLE

ALLAN R. HILTON, J.A.

JULIE DUTIL, J.A.

MARIE-FRANCE BICH, J.A.

JESSEL (JASON) BENJAMIN
MARCOVITZ

RESPONDENT

– Defendant

v.

STEPHANIE BRENDA BRUKER

RESPONDENT – INCIDENTAL
APPELLANT– Plaintiff

JUDGMENT

[
1
]

THE COURT: On appeal from a judgment of the
Superior Court, District of Montreal (the Honourable Mr. Justice Israel
Mass) rendered on March 28, 2003 that maintained the respondent's action
in part, condemned the appellant to pay the respondent $47,500 with interest
and the additional indemnity from the date of service of the respondent's
amended declaration, ordered a publication ban with respect to the names of the
parties and their two children and recommended that the publication ban be
respected beyond the jurisdiction of the Superior Court;

[
2
]

After having examined the file, heard the
parties and on the whole deliberated;

[
3
]

For the reasons of Hilton, J.A., with which
Dutil and Bich, JJ.A. agree:

[
4
]

ALLOWS
the appeal
without costs and dismisses the respondent's action, without costs;

[
5
]

DISMISSES
the
incidental appeal, without costs;

[
6
]

VACATES

paragraphs [61] and [62] in the conclusions of the judgment of the
Superior Court respecting a publication ban.

ALLAN R. HILTON, J.A.

JULIE
DUTIL, J.A.

MARIE-FRANCE
BICH, J.A.

Mtre Anne-France

Date of hearing:

February 15, 2005

REASONS OF HILTON, J.A.

INTRODUCTION

[
7
]

This appeal considers the enforceability of a
commonly seen provision in a consent to corollary relief amongst persons of the
Jewish faith that the parties signed in the context of their divorce case, and
whether an alleged breach of that provision by the former husband gives rise to
an action in damages by the former wife. The trial judge found the provision to
be enforceable and awarded damages to the plaintiff in the Superior Court.
[1]

The defendant in the Superior Court has appealed the judgment, while the
plaintiff seeks an increase in the amount of the condemnation by way of an
incidental appeal.

THE FACTUAL BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL CONTEXT

[
8
]

Stephanie Bruker was 20 years old and
attending Sir George Williams University
[2]
when she married
Jason Marcovitz in 1969. Ms. Bruker was a life‑long member of a
Conservative synagogue with Orthodox practices in Montreal, while
Mr. Marcovitz, who was then 32 years old and had been previously
married to the daughter of a rabbi, was a life‑long practising Orthodox Jew.
The parties were married in Ms. Bruker's synagogue.

[
9
]

After obtaining her undergraduate degree,
Ms. Bruker took an interior design program offered by the Montreal Museum
of Fine Arts, and then began to work as a self‑employed interior
designer. Mr. Marcovitz was an accountant in the employ of the Government
of Canada.

[
10
]

Initially, the parties lived in an apartment in
Côte Saint‑Luc, and then a spacious duplex in Hampstead. In June of 1979,
they purchased a luxurious home in Westmount. Despite efforts to have
Ms. Bruker conceive, the parties were unable to have children. They
eventually adopted two girls, one of whom was born in 1976, and the other in
1978.

[
11
]

In April of 1980, relatively soon after the
acquisition of the home in Westmount, Ms. Bruker initiated divorce
proceedings. Unbeknownst to Mr. Marcovitz, she had been involved in an
intermittent affair with someone she described as a former college sweetheart,
who also was Jewish, but who was married. During the course of her relationship
with this individual, she became pregnant, and in 1978, she had an abortion.

[
12
]

In their divorce file, experienced family law
counsel represented both Ms. Bruker and Mr. Marcovitz. With the
assistance of their counsel, by July of 1980 they reached an amicable agreement
on corollary measures ("the Consent"). Apart from the particular
provision in issue, the text of which is reproduced in paragraph [13]
below, the Consent recorded the parties' agreement on, amongst others, the
following issues:

●    Ms. Bruker
would have custody of the two children, with "liberal and flexible rights
of access and visitation … with the children, same to be exercised from time to
time by agreement between the parties";

●    Mr. Marcovitz
would vacate the common domicile in Westmount within 10 days of the
execution of the Consent, and that Ms. Bruker and the children would
continue to reside there until its sale, although she undertook to vacate it by
September 30, 1980, unless the parties had previously agreed in writing to
extend the delay;

●    Mr. Marcovitz
would begin to pay child support of $850 per month to Ms. Bruker, which
she agreed to use for their support and maintenance;

●    Mr. Marcovitz
would make a lump‑sum payment of $65,000 to Ms. Bruker from the
proceeds of sale of the common domicile in full and final settlement of all
alimentary and maintenance claims she might have against him;

●    apart from the
obligations set forth in the Consent, the parties agreed that they had no other
claims of any nature against each other, and therefore they each granted to the
other a "mutual, reciprocal, and irrevocable release, discharge and
waiver" of any such claims.

[
13
]

The provision that is the source of
Ms. Bruker's civil action, which in the Consent precedes the mutual
release to which I have referred in the previous paragraph, and which thus must
have been a factor in Ms. Bruker's decision to grant Mr. Marcovitz a
release, reads as follows:

The parties appear before the
Rabbinical authorities in the City and District of Montreal for the purpose of
obtaining the traditional religious Get,
[3]
immediately upon a
Decree Nisi of divorce being granted.

[
14
]

Boudreault, J. ratified the Consent
containing these provisions the day after its execution as part of an order of
provisional measures. It was again ratified and the parties were ordered to
conform to it as part of the Decree Nisi of Divorce Turmel, J. pronounced
on an uncontested basis on October 23, 1980.
[4]

[
15
]

Unfortunately, despite the rapidity with which
the parties had agreed on the resolution of all issues in July of 1980, their
relationship had deteriorated significantly by the time of the issuance of the
Decree Nisi in October that year. The reasons are not entirely clear, but it
seems that Mr. Marcovitz left the common residence at the behest of
Ms. Bruker earlier than he would have wanted.

[
16
]

Ms. Bruker enlisted the assistance of
friends, rabbis and family members of Mr. Marcovitz, but he would not
collaborate in the obtaining of a
ghet.
This meant that in the eyes of
her religion, Ms. Bruker was still married, and thus could not marry a man
who shared her religious faith. Had she nevertheless married a man, even
someone who was a non‑observant Jew, any children borne of the marriage
would be considered
mamzerim
, that is, bastards, and the ability of such
children to marry within the Orthodox Jewish faith would be limited to other
mamzerim
.
According to Ms. Bruker, not having a Jewish husband with similar beliefs
also deprived her from participating as fully as she would wish in various
religious and para‑religious activities. Her unenviable marital status
was that of an
agunah
, that is, she was bound to a dead marriage.

[
17
]

Through her counsel at the time, Ms. Bruker
also initiated contempt proceedings. A Special Rule pursuant to
articles 50 and following of the
Code of Civil Procedure
was issued
on November 22, 1982, but it could not be served properly because
according to the bailiff's return of service, Mr. Marcovitz refused to
open the door of the apartment in which he was living to accept service. The
Special Rule nevertheless came on for hearing before Lamb, J. on
January 21, 1983, and he dismissed it without any recorded reasons. No
contempt proceedings were ever renewed thereafter.

[
18
]

In the meantime, Ms. Bruker continued her
business activities as an interior designer in Montreal, and moved to other
homes in Westmount that she purchased and refurbished. She also began seeing
other men, some of whom were not Jewish and some of whom were married, and
having sexual relations with many of them.

[
19
]

As these events were unfolding, the divorce file
took a tumultuous turn for the worse, with innumerable proceedings and seizures
relating to child support. Despite the fact that he was supposed to have
"liberal and flexible rights of access and visitation" according to
the Consent, Mr. Marcovitz saw his daughters on an irregular basis, and
there was no civilised contact between the parties.

[
20
]

In 1989, Ms. Bruker moved to New York City,
where she pursued her career as an interior designer as an employee of an
architectural firm. One of the reasons that led her to move to New York was
that she felt there was a larger population of eligible Jewish men there
compared to Montreal, and she entertained the hope of meeting and marrying one
of them. She took steps to become integrated in the Conservative Jewish
community in New York, but she testified that her aim to meet a Jewish man
who she might marry was hampered by the fact that she was still considered to
be married despite her civil divorce, with the result that any eligible Jewish
man would not consider dating her for that reason alone. Nevertheless, as was
the case when she was in Montreal, Ms. Bruker did have a social life with
other men, which often included sexual relations.

[
21
]

Sadly, Ms. Bruker encountered a number of
problems with her daughters while in New York, and she appears to have
been estranged from them during their adolescence. One of them was taken away
from her and placed in a foster home. This too was a source of extensive
litigation in the United States that produced an unfavourable result for Ms.
Bruker. The other daughter ended up living in Colorado at a relatively early
age.

[
22
]

In July of 1989, Ms. Bruker began the civil
proceedings that are now before the Court. She concedes that she did so on the
advice of her attorney at the time and a rabbi as a means to pressure
Mr. Marcovitz into attending before a rabbinical tribunal for the purpose
of securing a
ghet
. As initially framed, the action was not one of
specific performance, but rather one of damages, in which a total of $500,000
was claimed. The damages alleged were $200,000 "for having been restrained
from going on with her life since the Decree Nisi of divorce", $200,000
"for having been restrained to remarry according to the Jewish
faith", and $100,000 "for having been restricted of having
children". Ms. Bruker also sent Mr. Marcovitz a demand letter on
November 12, 1990, after the lawsuit had begun, formally putting him on
notice to contact one of three named rabbis for the purpose of granting her a
ghet
.

[
23
]

Mr. Marcovitz contested the action on a
number of bases, including allegations to the effect that Ms. Bruker had
herself repudiated the Consent by seeking an increase in child support
payments. He also affirmed that Ms. Bruker was continuously harassing him
for money while at the same time alienating him from his daughters, and he
questioned her devotion to the Jewish faith. He added that as he was devoted to
the Jewish faith, his refusal to go before the rabbinical authorities was a
matter of conscience. He later amended his defence in 1994 to assert that he
had offered to grant a
ghet
upon a discontinuance of the action, but
that Ms. Bruker had refused and had insisted on a financial settlement as
a condition of accepting a
ghet
.

[
24
]

It should be noted here that Parliament amended
the
Divorce Act
[5]

in 1990 to add
section 21.1
,
[6]
the effect of
which, insofar as possibly relevant to this case, provided a means to someone
in the position of Ms. Bruker to have a religious barrier removed which it
was within the power of a former spouse to remove by dismissing or striking a
proceeding brought by the former spouse under the
Divorce Act,
[7]

unless the former spouse removed the
barrier in question.
Section 21.1
only operates, however, if the former
spouse initiates a proceeding, and not otherwise. Therefore, to the extent that
this provision provided any potential relief to Ms. Bruker, it was of no
use to her in the absence of a proceeding initiated by Mr. Marcovitz.
Nevertheless, Ms. Bruker did file a section 21.1 affidavit dated
December 3, 1990 in the record of the divorce case.

[
25
]

Mr. Marcovitz finally appeared before the
rabbinical tribunal with Ms. Bruker on December 5, 1995, and the
three rabbis issued the
ghet
. More than 15 years had intervened
between the Decree Nisi and the issuance of the
ghet
, by which time
Ms. Bruker was almost 47 years old.

[
26
]

There is a dispute between the parties as to
whether Ms. Bruker's section 21.1 affidavit had any bearing on
Mr. Marcovitz' decision to appear before the rabbinical authorities.
Mr. Marcovitz had presented a motion in the divorce file dated
November 1, 1995 in which he sought to annul his obligation to pay child
support to Ms. Bruker retroactive to the date that each child had stopped
living with her, along with two other conclusions seeking interim relief, one
of which was to suspend the execution of a seizure by garnishment practised by
Ms. Bruker's former counsel.

[
27
]

When his motion came on for hearing before
Marcelin, J. on November 21, 1995, the latter conclusion was granted,
however, Marcelin, J. refused to hear the substantive conclusion seeking
annulment of the child support obligations. It was only after that hearing that
Mr. Marcovitz appeared before the rabbinical tribunal and the
ghet

was issued. He contends, however, that by then, irrespective of the refusal of
Marcelin, J. to hear the most important conclusion of his motion on
November 21, he was content with the financial and other arrangements with
his children such that he felt liberated from Ms. Bruker, and therefore he
collaborated in the issuance of the
ghet
.
[8]

[
28
]

Having now obtained the
ghet
, however,
Ms. Bruker did not let bygones be bygones. On June 21, 1996, she
amended her declaration and increased the amount of her claim to $1,350,000 by
adding a claim of $750,000 for loss of consortium.

[
29
]

After four days of trial had been completed,
Mr. Marcovitz both attacked the constitutionality of
section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
[9]
on the basis that it unlawfully interfered with the exercise of his
freedom of religion and was discriminatory, and, he amended his defence. The
constitutional challenge was never adjudicated, and the parties agreed to
proceed for the purposes of the action as if the impugned provision did not
exist. Nevertheless, paragraphs 35 to 39 inclusively of the Amended
Defence to Amended Declaration set out the legal as opposed to factual basis on
which Mr. Marcovitz contends Ms. Bruker's action should be dismissed.
These paragraphs read as follows:

35. Defendant respectfully
represents that his undertaking
[10]
to appear before
the Beth Din
[11]
constituted a moral obligation, and not a legal one, and this
obligation is simply not justiciable in civil law. This undertaking can in no
way be interpreted as a limitation as to the representations Defendant could
have made before the religious authorities;

36. The continued existence of this
lawsuit constitutes a breach of Defendant's freedom of religion and conscience;

37. This lawsuit has a veneer of
acceptability for no other reason than the existence of
section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
, by the terms of which the federal government sought to
bring the Ghet into the domain of the civil law, and this section is
unconstitutional for all the reasons set out in the Notice to the Attorney‑General
which has been served herein;

38. If the Agreement
[12]

is one to attend before the Beth Din as an arbitration tribunal, then this is
illegal at civil law; if the Agreement is specifically to attend before the
Beth Din for a religious divorce, then it is outside the reach of the civil law
and is not justiciable and any compulsion, by injunction or damages, to give
civil effect to such Agreement is an unconstitutional impingement on
Defendant's freedom of religion;

39. In any event, it is only the
Beth Din which can morally determine whether Defendant has respected or transgressed
his religious obligations flowing from the circumstances of the breakdown of
the marriage and the Agreement signed thereafter; if the civil court attempts
to do so, there is impingement on Defendant's freedom of religion.

THE JUDGMENT OF THE SUPERIOR COURT

[
30
]

The trial judge awarded Ms. Bruker $47,500,
with interest and the additional indemnity from the date of the service of the
amended declaration in June of 1996. He concluded that the inclusion of
paragraph 12 in the Consent, which I have reproduced in
paragraph [13] of these reasons, made the obligation it stated one of a
civil contract, albeit with religious undertones, which Mr. Marcovitz had
breached by not attending before the rabbinical authorities immediately after
the granting of the Decree Nisi. Since a
ghet
was issued without
incident in 1995, the trial judge reasoned that one would also have been issued
without incident in 1980, even though the circumstances of fact had changed
dramatically between 1980 and 1995.

[
31
]

There were two components of the damages. First,
the trial judge found that Ms. Bruker was entitled to $2,500 for each of
the 15 years she did not have her
ghet,
which represented a
restraint on her ability to remarry according to the precepts of Orthodox
Judaism. He also awarded her $10,000 for not having been able to have a
legitimate child "under the precept of the Orthodox Jewish community to
which she belonged". The trial judge's characterization of Ms. Bruker
as being an Orthodox Jewess was an error that both parties readily acknowledge
in that she contended that she had always been a member of Conservative
synagogues in Montreal and New York, with the one in Montreal having
Orthodox practices.

[
32
]

The trial judge also held that interest and the
additional indemnity should not run from the date of the institution of the
action in 1989 but only from the date of the amended proceedings in 1996, since
Ms. Bruker had testified that her primary objective in bringing the action
in 1989 was not to obtain damages, but rather to force Mr. Marcovitz to
respect the obligation he had undertaken in the Consent.

ISSUES IN APPEAL

[
33
]

Mr. Marcovitz seeks the reversal of the
judgment of the Superior Court and the dismissal of Ms. Bruker's action.
For her part, Ms. Bruker solicits an increase of the damages awarded to
the amount claimed in her action as amended in 1996, that is, $1,350,000.

[
34
]

Mr. Marcovitz argues in appeal principally
that:

●    his presence before
the rabbinical authorities in Montreal was unnecessary, and that
Ms. Bruker had other means at her disposal to obtaining a
ghet
, or,
alternatively, that she could have obtained a religious annulment which would
have achieved the desired objective of enabling her to meet eligible Jewish men
and to marry one of them;

●    the claim is not
justiciable by secular courts in light of the religious nature of the
obligation, and in any event, as a matter of public policy, civil claims in
damages do not lie for an alleged breach of an order issued in the context of a
divorce file;

●    there was no causal
relationship between the failure of Mr. Marcovitz to appear before the
rabbinical authorities in 1980 and any of the damages claimed by
Ms. Bruker, including those awarded by the trial judge, inasmuch as it
cannot be assumed that the
ghet
would not have been contested in 1980 in
light of the facts then existing, even though it was uncontested in 1995 by
which time  the facts had changed;

●    there was no
evidence that the absence of a
ghet
was the direct cause of the failure
of Ms. Bruker to remarry an eligible Jewish man since she never presented
a "flesh and blood suitor" willing to marry her, and that in any
event, Ms. Bruker's sexual conduct with another man during the marriage,
including an abortion, and with other men after the civil divorce, is
incompatible with someone who contends to be an observant practitioner of her
faith, since such conduct is proscribed by the precepts of that faith.

[
35
]

As for Ms. Bruker, she asserts that:

●    the trial judge was
correct in his analysis as to the enforceability of the obligation, which
became civil once it was incorporated into the Consent, and the breach of which
gives rise to an assessment of resulting damages;

●    her sexual conduct
with other men, while not consistent with the precepts of Conservative Judaism,
does not mean that she is not a devout practitioner of her faith;

●    that there were no
other alternatives to her becoming free to marry an eligible Jewish man apart
from Mr. Marcovitz respecting the obligation he freely contracted in the
Consent;

●    the evidence
demonstrates that not having a
ghet
prevented Ms. Bruker from even
meeting and dating, let alone marrying, an eligible Jewish man;

●    the trial judge
nevertheless erred in limiting her damages to the amount awarded, which should
be substantially increased, and he further erred by not awarding interest and
the additional indemnity from the date of the institution of the proceedings in
1989.

[
36
]

Although it is apparent that the appeal presents
a number of difficult issues for consideration, I believe that the case can be
resolved by focussing primarily on the nature of the obligation set out in
paragraph 12 of the Consent.

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION

[
37
]

For ease of reference, I reproduce again paragraph 12
of the Consent:

The parties appear before the
Rabbinical authorities in the City and District of Montreal for the purpose of
obtaining the traditional religious Get, immediately upon a Decree Nisi of
Divorce being granted.

[
38
]

It is important immediately to distinguish such
a provision in a consent from the others that I have mentioned in paragraph
[12] above.

[
39
]

The latter are properly matters that deal with
issues that might come before a court adjudicating a divorce case, such as the
determination of Mr. Marcovitz' rights of access and visiting rights with
his children, the extent of child support and the agreement of a spouse to pay
a lump‑sum amount to the other spouse in satisfaction of all alimentary
claims. Similarly, many of such issues are also subject to variation,
rescission or suspension pursuant to
section 17
of the
Divorce Act
[13]

once the divorce is pronounced.

[
40
]

Indeed, the divorce file of the parties is
replete with motions under the auspices of that provision.

[
41
]

The appearance before rabbinical authorities for
the purpose of obtaining a
ghet
, as mentioned in paragraph 12 of
the Consent, however, is not one that could be properly obtained as an order of
corollary relief at the initiative of a party to a divorce. Even now, the most
that could ever be sought is the relief contemplated by
section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
,
[14]

which, as we have seen, is imperfect,
since its implementation is dependent on the presentation of an unrelated
motion by a spouse who has it within his or her power to remove a barrier to
obtaining a religious divorce by effectively subjecting the court's
consideration of the unrelated motion to the removal of the religious barrier.

[
42
]

What then does the text of paragraph 12 of
the Consent mean?

[
43
]

First, despite a somewhat fainthearted argument
by counsel for Mr. Marcovitz, I do not consider that the term
"Rabbinical authorities" was uncertain to the point of not being
susceptible of being understood by him. I concede that for someone who is not a
practitioner of the Jewish faith, or who has not read the record of this case
in appeal, the precise meaning of the term would not be immediately understood.
Throughout their respective factums, however, the parties have continuously
referred to the
Beth Din
as the rabbinical tribunal that issues a
ghet
.
So too did the trial judge in his judgment, as did the parties in their
evidence, and the experts who filed reports and were called upon to testify. In
addition, to the extent there might have been any confusion, Mr. Marcovitz
was able to overcome it easily when he eventually decided to appear before the
Beth
Din
in Montreal when the
ghet
was eventually issued. He also seems
to have managed to find his way to the
Beth Din
for the issuance of a
ghet

after he was civilly divorced from his first wife.

[
44
]

I therefore have no doubt that had he been of a
mind to participate in a process in October of 1980 that could have led to the
issuance of a
ghet
, he would have known exactly what to do.

[
45
]

The more important issue, however, has to do
with the substance of the obligation.

[
46
]

The expert evidence makes it clear that
participating in the process that may lead to the issuance of a
ghet
is
religious in nature, which is consistent with the concept of a religious
divorce. That is also the implicit conclusion of the trial judge, even though
he characterized it as a civil obligation because of the form of the agreement.
It is not simply a matter of "showing up" and going through a
meaningless ritual, especially for someone who is an Orthodox Jew. A religious intention
is required. Indeed, divorcing by a formal written document is considered
amongst the 613
mitzvot
or commandments from the Torah.
[15]

[
47
]

Ms. Bruker and Mr. Marcovitz do not dispute that
the very first item of business when the
Beth Din
is convened is for the

dayanim
[16]

to confirm that the parties are before
them on a purely voluntary basis. Any previous consent to do so, however valid
or freely given it may have been at the time, is of no consequence.
[17]

In fact, a party who has previously given a consent must renounce it.
Therefore, the process of obtaining a
ghet
would come to a halt if a
party were to state that he or she was present before the
Beth Din
as a
result of a court order or some other form of compulsion, unless that party
then

consented to the process.

[
48
]

Next, counsel for Ms. Bruker informed the
Court during oral argument that the obligation of Mr. Marcovitz in the
circumstances he undertook in paragraph 12 of the Consent obliged him not
only to actually appear at the
Beth Din
, but also to do what was necessary
before the
dayanim
to facilitate the
ghet
being issued. That
would be consistent with his appearance before the
Beth Din
being
"for the purpose of obtaining the traditional religious Get", to use
the actual words of the Consent. Thus, this argument posits that the agreement
to do so would necessarily have been pre‑ordained at the time of the
execution of the Consent, irrespective of whatever reason of religious
conscience the obligated party might then have, if any, not to facilitate the
obtaining of the
ghet
.

[
49
]

In these circumstances, does Mr. Marcovitz'
refusal to respect the agreement that he signed in July of 1980 mean that he
has exposed himself to damages, or, does the nature of the obligation stray
into the domain of religion that is normally beyond the ken of the secular
courts?

[
50
]

Traditionally, Canadian courts have been loathe
to become involved in disputes between persons of a religion that involve
questions relating to their religious beliefs, or enforcement of religious
rights or obligations against each other or against religious authorities, even
before the adoption of the
Canadian Charter of Rights

and
Freedoms.
This can be seen in family law and other contexts as well.

[
51
]

An early illustration of that reticence is
evident from the case of
Després
v.
Séminaire de Québec
[18]
,
where Lemieux, C.J. held that a plaintiff in a civil case could not invoke
canon law against the defendant seminary to argue that it was prevented from
asserting a ground of defence inconsistent with canon law.

[
52
]

In a case bearing some resemblance to the
circumstance of this appeal, a majority judgment of the Manitoba Court of
Appeal in
Morris
v.
Morris
[19]
reversed a
judgment of the Court of Queen's Bench and dismissed an action brought by an
Orthodox Jewish woman against her ex‑husband from whom she had been
divorced civilly. The former wife had sought a declaration and an order of
mandamus based on a religious pre‑nuptial contract
[20]
that she was
entitled to an order against the former husband to institute appropriate
proceedings before a religious tribunal to obtain a
ghet
.

[
53
]

Only the dissenting judge, Freedman, C.J.,
was of the view that the former wife's claim was essentially one for the
enforcement of contractual rights, even though the contract was a religious and
not a secular one.
[21]
This analysis resembles that of the trial judge in this case. The
four judges in the majority, albeit for different reasons, held that a secular
court could not make the order requested which they found to be essentially of
a religious nature.

[
54
]

Not long after the coming into force of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and

Freedoms
, in
Baxter
v.
Baxter
,
[22]

a man of the Roman Catholic faith sought to avoid a decree absolute of divorce
being pronounced against him on the basis that to do so would amount to an
interference with his religious belief, which included the admonitions from the
Scriptures to the effect that "What therefore God hath joined together,
let not man put asunder"
[23]
and "For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law
to her husband so long as he liveth".
[24]

[
55
]

Pennell, J. granted the decree absolute of
divorce and held that public policy was to the effect that marriage was a civil
agreement that parties could enter into in accordance with the religious
scruples or canons of their church, and that its civil dissolution did not
infringe the defendant's freedom of religion that was protected by the
Canadian
Charter
.

[
56
]

In
Kaddoura
v.
Hammoud
,
[25]

Rutherford, J. granted an application for divorce of a man and woman
married pursuant to the Muslim faith, but dismissed the wife's counter‑claim
for the payment of a sum of money due to her under a marriage contract entered
into according to the Islamic religion on the basis that the husband's
obligation was religious in nature and therefore should not be entertained by a
secular court. The obligation in question, known as a
Mahr
, was
described as having its roots in the Holy
Qur'an
, as being essential to
a Muslim marriage, and without which there would be no Muslim marriage. In the
course of his reasons, Rutherford, J. said this:

The Mahr and the extent to which it
obligates a husband to make payment to his wife is essentially and
fundamentally an Islamic religious matter. Because Mahr is a religious matter,
the resolution of any dispute relating to it or the consequences of failing to
honour the obligation are also religious in their content and context. While
not, perhaps, an ideal comparison, I cannot help but think that the obligation
of the Mahr is as unsuitable for adjudication in the civil courts as is an obligation
in a Christian religious marriage such as to love, honour and cherish, or to
remain faithful, or to maintain the marriage in sickness or other adversity so
long as both parties live, or to raise children according to specified
religious doctrine. Many such promises go well beyond the basic legal
commitment to marriage required by our civil law, and are essentially matters
of chosen religion and morality. They are derived from and are dependent upon
doctrine and faith. They bind the conscience as a matter of religious principle
but not necessarily as a matter of enforceable civil law.
[26]

[
57
]

According to Rutherford, J., adjudicating
the wife's counter‑claim would, "necessarily lead the Court into the
'religious thicket',
[27]
a place that the courts cannot safely and should not go."
[28]

[
58
]

The same reticence has been seen in a commercial
context.

[
59
]

In
Levitt's Kosher

Foods Inc.
v.

Levin et al
.,
[29]
Benotto, J.
of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice permanently stayed an action brought
by the plaintiff, a company producing and selling kosher meat, against three
rabbis who were part of a council in Toronto responsible for the certification
of establishments to ensure their compliance with Jewish dietary laws. She held
that although the plaintiff's claim, which was based on restraint of trade
amongst other grounds, appeared to be in relation to property and civil rights,
it was in reality an attack on religious policies flowing from their
implementation by the defendant rabbis. She concluded that the real issue was
one of "religious belief and conscience", the continuance of which
"would work an injustice to the defendants because the claims are not
justiciable and are thus oppressive, vexatious, and an abuse of process".
[30]

[
60
]

Finally, the recent judgment of the Supreme
Court of Canada in
Syndicat Northcrest
v.
Amselem
[31]
warrants consideration.

[
61
]

Amongst the precise issues before the Court were
whether a provision in the by‑laws of a declaration of co‑ownership
that prohibited decorations, alterations or constructions on the balconies of
the residential building in which the appellants lived infringed their freedom
of religion as guaranteed under
section 3
of the
Quebec
Charter of
Human Rights and Freedoms
[32]

to erect
succahs
[33]

on their balconies during the nine‑day period of the year, and, whether
the appellants had effectively waived their rights when they signed the
declaration of co‑ownership. The majority of the Court concluded that the
impairment of the appellants' religious freedom was serious and the intrusion
on the respondent's contractual rights minimal, and that while the issue of
whether a guaranteed right such as freedom of religion could be validly waived
was not free from doubt, on the facts of the case before the Court, it had not
been shown that the purported waiver was "voluntary, freely expressed and
with a clear understanding of the true consequences and effects of so
doing".
[34]

[
62
]

The Court therefore allowed the appeal and
declared that the appellants were entitled to erect
succahs
on their
balconies during
Succot
, subject to a variety of undertakings they had
given.

[
63
]

In the course of his reasons, Iacobucci, J.
said this about the nature of religion in the context of freedom of religion:

While it is perhaps not
possible to define religion precisely, some outer definition is useful since
only beliefs, convictions and practices rooted in religion, as opposed to those
that are secular, socially based or conscientiously held, are protected by the
guarantee of freedom of religion. Defined broadly, religion typically involves
a particular and comprehensive system of faith and worship. Religion also tends
to involve the belief in a divine, superhuman or controlling power. In essence,
religion is about freely and deeply held personal convictions or beliefs
connected to an individual's spiritual faith and integrally linked to one's
self‑definition and spiritual fulfilment, the practices of which allow
individuals to foster a connection with the divine or with the subject or
object of that spiritual faith.
[35]

[
64
]

Iacobucci, J. also made the following
observation in speaking about the nature of the guarantee of freedom of
religion that I find to be particularly apposite to the circumstances of this
case:

In my view, the State is in no
position to be, nor should it become, the arbiter of religious dogma.
Accordingly, courts should avoid judicially interpreting and thus determining,
either explicitly or implicitly, the content of a subjective understanding of
religious requirement, "obligation", precept,
"commandment", custom or ritual. Secular judicial determinations of
theological or religious disputes, or of contentious matters of religious
doctrine, unjustifiably entangle the court in the affairs of religion.
[36]

[
65
]

In support of the conclusion reached by the
trial judge that the obligation contained in paragraph 12 of the Consent
was enforceable, counsel for Ms. Bruker drew the Court's attention to
judgments rendered in state courts in the United States, as well as one from
the English Court of Appeal. I approach the American judgments with some caution,
however, as they are both fact‑specific and engage considerations of law
that are not necessarily applicable to the circumstances of this case. Insofar
as the English judgment is concerned, it bears no factual or legal relationship
to the issues under review here.

[
66
]

In the United States, based on the evidence
presented in one case, a
ghet
was not considered to be of a religious
nature. In another case, the pleadings soliciting an order that a former
husband obtain a
ghet
were judged to state a valid cause of action.

[
67
]

In
Minkin
v.
Minkin
,
[37]
Minuskin, J. of the Supreme Court of New Jersey, Chancery
Division, concluded, in the context of a case involving the First Amendment to
the United States Constitution
[38]
and a claim by a civilly divorced Jewish woman for an order
requiring her husband to obtain and pay for a
ghet
, that a
ghet

is not a religious act. In
Minkin
, the parties were married in a Jewish
ceremony and signed a
ketubah
in which they agreed to comply with the
laws of Moses and Israel, which includes securing a
ghet
.
Minuskin, J. said the following about the evidence before him:

Relying upon credible expert
testimony that the acquisition of a get is not a religious act, the court finds
that the entry of an order compelling defendant to secure a get would have the
clear secular purpose of completing a dissolution of the marriage. Its primary
effect neither advances nor inhibits religion since it does not require the
husband to participate in a religious ceremony or to do acts contrary to his
religious beliefs. Nor would the order be an excessive entanglement with
religion. In addition to testimony to that effect, the court takes judicial
notice that the Legislature has seen fit to authorize clergy to perform
marriages and, in doing so, permits the use of a religious ceremony. See
N.J.S.A. 37:1-13. Such conduct, as sanctioned by the Legislature, has never
been considered to be an excessive entanglement with religion. The get
procedure is a release document devoid of religious connotation and cannot be
construed as any more religious than the marriage ceremony itself. Thus, the
three‑prong test protecting defendant pursuant to the First Amendment is
satisfied. The court concludes that it may, without infringing on his
constitutional rights, order defendant to specifically perform his contract.
[39]

[
68
]

It is not apparent, however, from a reading of
this case, that the parties were practitioners of the same branches of Judaism
as Ms. Bruker and Mr. Marcovitz. This is of some importance in
assessing the weight to be given to the finding on the evidence of
Minuskin, J., since the evidence in this case showed that the standards
and requirements for a
ghet
are not uniform within the various branches
of Judaism. It is also obvious that a finding of fact by a trial judge in one case
cannot influence, let alone control, findings in another case, where the
evidence may be wholly or partially different.

[
69
]

In the case of
Avitzur
v.
Avitzur
,
[40]

the Court of Appeals of New York, that state's highest court, in a sharply
divided judgment, upheld a general enforcement of a clause in a
ketubah

that stipulated that in the event of a civil divorce, the husband would grant a

ghet
. The issue arose in the context of an appeal from an order of the
Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that had granted a former husband's
motion to dismiss a complaint (that is, an action) taken by his former wife to
compel him to appear before a rabbinical tribunal to obtain a religious
divorce. The Court of Appeals reversed the order of the Appellate Division and
reinstated the former wife's action.

[
70
]

The parties were married between 1966 and 1978.
In May of 1978 the husband was granted a civil divorce. The ex‑wife then
sought to summon her ex‑husband before the
Beth Din
relying upon
their
ketubah
in which he had promised that if they were to divorce he
would appear before the
Beth Din
for matters concerning their marriage,
including that of a
ghet
. The four judges who formed the majority of the
Court, speaking through Wachtler, J., concluded that the
ketubah

qualified as an ante‑nuptial agreement, was valid and enforceable:

The present case can be decided
solely upon the application of neutral principles of contract law, without
reference to any religious principle. Consequently, defendant's objections to
enforcement of his promise to appear before the Beth Din, based as they are
upon the religious origin of the agreement, pose no constitutional barrier to
the relief sought by plaintiff. The fact that the agreement was entered into as
part of a religious ceremony does not render it unenforceable. Solemnization of
the marital relationship often takes place in accordance with the religious
beliefs of the participants, and this State has long recognized this religious
aspect by permitting duly authorized pastors, rectors, priests, rabbis and
other religious officials to perform the ceremony (
Domestic Relations Law, §
11
, subds 1, 7). Similarly, that the obligations undertaken by the parties
to the Ketubah are grounded in religious belief and practice does not preclude
enforcement of its secular terms. Nor does the fact that all of the Ketubah's
provisions may not be judicially recognized prevent the court from enforcing
that portion of the agreement by which the parties promised to refer their
disputes to a nonjudicial forum (
see Ferro v Bologna, 31 NY2d 30, 36
).
The courts may properly enforce so much of this agreement as is not in
contravention of law or public policy.

In short, the relief sought by
plaintiff in this action is simply to compel defendant to perform a secular obligation
to which he contractually bound himself. In this regard, no doctrinal issue
need be passed upon, no implementation of a religious duty is contemplated, and
no interference with religious authority will result. Certainly nothing the
Beth Din can do would in any way affect the civil divorce. To the extent that
an enforceable promise can be found by the application of neutral principles of
contract law, plaintiff will have demonstrated entitlement to the relief
sought. Consideration of other substantive issues bearing upon plaintiff's
entitlement to a religious divorce, however, is appropriately left to the forum
the parties chose for resolving the matter.
[41]

[
71
]

Jones, J., dissenting on his own behalf and
that of two colleagues, was of the opinion that there was no reason to believe
that when the parties signed the
ketubah
they wanted to endow it with
civil or secular effects:

At the outset we observe that the
complaint contains no allegation that the parties intended that the Ketubah
should manifest secular promises or have any civil or secular status or any
legal significance independent of the religious ceremony between them of which
it was an integral part. Nor is any such assertion advanced in the papers
submitted by the wife in support of her cross motion for summary judgment.

Moreover, it appears evident to us
that any determination of the content and particulars of the rights of the wife
or the obligations of the husband under this document cannot be made without
inquiry into and resolution of questions of Jewish religious law and tradition.
We think it inaccurate to identify the relief sought by plaintiff, as does the
majority, as "simply to compel defendant to perform a secular obligation
to which he contractually bound himself.
[42]

[
72
]

In addition, according to Jones, J., it was
not possible to determine if the husband had an obligation to appear before the

Beth Din
without referring to religious and ecclesiastical law. It
"would necessarily violate the constitutional prohibition against
entanglement of our secular courts in matters of religious and ecclesiastical
content":

Nothing in the record
suggests that it was the intention of the parties when they signed this
religious document that the civil courts of the State of New York were to have
jurisdiction to determine the substantive rights created thereby or to invoke
civil procedures and remedies for the enforcement of such rights. Indeed, any
conclusion on the part of our courts that this express provision was not
intended by the parties as the exclusive remedy available to them for any
breach of their obligations under the Ketubah would itself necessarily entail
examination of Jewish law and tradition.
[43]

[
73
]

It should be noted immediately that the judgment
in
Avitzur
was rendered only on the basis of the pleadings and without
the benefit of any expert evidence as to the religious nature of a
ghet
,
contrary to what is the case here, where expert evidence and related documents
as well as expert testimony formed part of the record.

[
74
]

Our Court was also referred to the judgment of
the English Court of Appeal in
Brett v. Brett
,
[44]
in which the
failure of a husband to grant a
ghet
to his young Orthodox Jewish ex‑wife
from whom he had been civilly divorced was taken into account as a factor in a
claim by the ex‑wife for maintenance and a lump payment sum under the
provisions of the
Matrimonial Causes Act, 1965
. The rationale was that
it seemed probable that the ex‑husband would persist in denying a
ghet

to his ex‑wife, with the result that she would be precluded from marrying
some other man who would be able to support her.

[
75
]

As I mentioned in paragraph [65], these
circumstances of fact and law are obviously not relevant to the principal issue
to be decided in this appeal.

* * * * *

[
76
]

Although one cannot help but be sympathetic to
the plight of a Jewish woman whose former husband delays or denies her a
ghet
,
whether or not he has entered into a premarital agreement to do so or in the
context of a consent to corollary relief, I have concluded that the substance
of the former husband's obligation is religious in nature, irrespective of the
form in which the obligation is stated, and accordingly, that an alleged breach
of the obligation is not enforceable by the secular courts to obtain damages or
specific performance. Manifestly, it is not the role of secular courts to
palliate the discriminatory effect of the absence of a
ghet
on a Jewish
woman who wants to obtain one, any more than it would be appropriate for
secular courts, in an extra‑contractual context, to become involved in similar
disputes involving other religions where unequal treatment is the fate of women
in terms of their access to positions in the clergy, or as we have seen
recently in other contexts, the fate reserved for same‑sex couples being
denied the right to marry in religious ceremonies of some religious faiths. The
same would also be true of a court's reticence, for example, in a contractual
context, to compel compliance with an undertaking in a consent to corollary
measures for a party not to contest an ecclesiastical annulment when that party
had legitimate grounds to oppose the annulment.

[
77
]

In addition to being entirely consistent with
the Canadian judicial approach that uniformly seeks to distance secular courts
from becoming involved in disputes between parties that are internal to their
religions, while at the same time respecting the fundamental principles of
freedom of religion and the exercise of religious conscience, I believe that
such a result also flows from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Amselem
,
[45]

some extracts from the reasons of Iacobucci, J. I have reproduced in
paragraphs [63] and [64]. If an observant Jewish man could not be presumed to
have contractually waived his freedom of religion and thus be entitled to erect
a
succah
on his balcony, how can Mr. Marcovitz be presumed to have
waived his right not to appear before a rabbinical tribunal for the granting of
a
ghet
as a matter of religious conscience, and who is this Court to
tell him that he had a civil duty to perform irrespective of the rights he
might have according to his religious beliefs?

[
78
]

The purpose of freedom of religion or the
exercise of religious freedom should not be interpreted as having a coercive
component. In essence, freedom of religion is a fundamental personal right.
Canadian courts do not have the protection of religions
per se
as
part of their mission. Rather, recourse can be had to Canadian courts to ensure
that individuals can act in accordance with their religious beliefs, subject to
laws of general application that satisfy provisions such as
section 1
of
the
Canadian Charter
.

[
79
]

In this case, Ms. Bruker does not seek the
Court's protection for the exercise of her freedom of religion. Instead, she
seeks to be indemnified for Mr. Marcovitz' failure, from her perspective,
to perform a religious act that the evidence shows he could not be compelled to
perform and could only perform voluntarily, despite a pre‑existing
undertaking to do so.

[
80
]

To condemn Mr. Marcovitz to pay damages in
such circumstances would be inconsistent with the recognition of his right to
execute his religious beliefs or duties as he sees fit without curial
intervention.

[
81
]

The difficulty of secular courts considering the
effect of factual arguments relating to religion is also apparent from at least
one of Mr. Marcovitz' affirmative defences. He alleges at paragraph 9
of his most recently amended defence that Ms. Bruker "has never been
a particularly devout adherent of the Jewish faith" and that her
"alleged religious attachment was never brought forward with any kind of
insistence until the latter part of 1989", that is to say when she began
her legal proceedings in this case. The evidence is also replete with
references to Ms. Bruker's sexual activity after her civil divorce. In the
context of examining the issue of causation, Mr. Marcovitz argues in his
factum that "the essence of the sanctity of a Jewish marriage is
predicated upon fidelity", and that "the concept of fidelity is
foreign" to Ms. Bruker. I appreciate that these defences flow from
the nature of Ms. Bruker's claim for damages. In my opinion, however, it
is highly inappropriate for secular courts to be called upon in the context of
an action in damages for breach of contract to be asked to measure the nature
of a person's conduct on the depth of that person's religiosity, an exercise
the Court would have been bound to undertake had it considered Ms. Bruker's
claim to be justiciable.

[
82
]

Moreover, in my respectful view, at least some
of the bases on which the trial judge predicated his finding that
Mr. Marcovitz had engaged his civil liability are erroneous.

[
83
]

I have already mentioned that in my opinion, the
substance of the obligation was religious and not secular with religious
undertones, as the trial judge held. Quebec civil law places emphasis on the
substance of obligations, and not the form in which they are expressed,
[46]

unless the form of an agreement is an essential component of its validity, such
as would be the case with a hypothec on immoveable property
[47]

or a marriage contract.
[48]
That is not the situation with which we are faced.

[
84
]

It matters not that the obligation was stated in
the Consent that the Superior Court ratified, since the Superior Court could
never have entertained an application for corollary relief under

section 17
of the
Divorce Act
[49]
to require the
issuance of a
ghet
. It is not at all unusual to see the parties in an
agreement on corollary relief undertake to perform a variety of obligations
that are not, strictly speaking, obtainable independently, but which are
desirable nevertheless to the extent that they promote an amicable post‑divorce
environment.

[
85
]

While I recognize the usefulness of the
inclusion of obligations of this nature in divorce agreements, it does not
follow that they all automatically become subject to curial supervision and
control, whether for specific performance or damages in the event of a breach.
In my view, in order for such clauses to be enforceable, they must be directly
related to one of the subject matters on which courts issue or vary orders of
corollary relief, and otherwise be justiciable. A simple illustration would be
a clause in which a non-custodial parent refused to respect an obligation in a
consent not to smoke in front of an acutely asthmatic child, in which case that
parent's rights of access might well be reduced or be made subject to
supervision. Absent such circumstances, I do not see how the parties can
consensually confer jurisdiction on the Superior Court on a subject matter for
which Parliament did not provide in the
Divorce Act
.
[50]

That is why I believe that Ms. Bruker could never have properly obtained
an order of specific performance in her divorce file requiring
Mr. Marcovitz to appear before the Rabbinical authorities, although she
may have had grounds to contend in the divorce file that her consent to the
mutual release that was also part of the Consent may have been vitiated.

[
86
]

The trial judge also concluded that since a
ghet

was issued in 1995, one would therefore have been issued after the Decree
Nisi had been issued in 1980. As I mentioned in paragraph [15], the
prevailing situation between the parties had changed dramatically from the time
the Consent was signed in July of 1980 and the time the Decree Nisi was granted
in October of 1980. Mr. Marcovitz' undoubtedly signed the Consent
willingly at the time, but as the evidence shows, as I referred to in
paragraph [47], the fact of such a consent would not only be completely
irrelevant to the rabbinical authorities, he would have had to renounce that
consent and stipulate that what he was
then
doing was voluntary. Since,
manifestly according to the evidence, that would not have been the case, the
ghet

could not have been issued.

[
87
]

The position of Ms. Bruker that I mentioned
in paragraph [48] that the terms of the Consent obliged Mr. Marcovitz
both to appear before the rabbinical authorities and to do what was necessary
to facilitate the issuance of the
ghet
cannot possibly be reconciled
with what I understand to be the exercise of his religious conscience. Indeed,
the position of Ms. Bruker suggests that in essence, Mr. Marcovitz
would have to be untruthful as to the voluntary nature of his presence before
the
Beth Din
as well as his willingness to grant the
ghet
,

if
that was what was required in order to have it issued. In such a case, an obligation
cannot be legally enforceable that requires the debtor of the obligation to be
untruthful in what are undoubtedly solemn religious circumstances.

[
88
]

In my opinion, the most that can be said from a
civil law perspective of the obligation in paragraph 12 of the Consent is
that it is a moral obligation. The learned authors Baudouin and Jobin describe
such obligations this way, in contrast to civil obligations:

L'obligation
civile est sanctionnée par la loi, ce qui permet au créancier d'en exiger l'exécution
devant les tribunaux. À celle-ci, on oppose l'obligation morale qui se situe en
dehors du domaine juridique, qui n'est pas sanctionnée par le législateur et
dont le pouvoir contraignant relève uniquement du for intérieur, c'est‑à‑dire
du remords. Le «créancier» d'une obligation morale n'en peut poursuivre
l'exécution devant les tribunaux, car elle n'est susceptible que d'exécution
volontaire.
[51]

[
89
]

Similarly, the learned authors Pineau, Burman
and Gaudet speak of a moral obligation as being one of "le devoir de
morale, le devoir de conscience".
[52]

[
90
]

These considerations more aptly describe what
Mr. Marcovitz undertook to do, and explain why civil courts should refuse
to become involved in assessing whether there has been a breach of the
obligation. If there is any relief available to Ms. Bruker, it is in a
religious forum, not a secular one.

[
91
]

I am therefore bound to conclude that
Mr. Marcovitz' appeal should be allowed and the action of Ms. Bruker
dismissed. In light of the nature of the proceedings and their novelty, I would
do so without costs in this Court and in the Superior Court.

THE INCIDENTAL APPEAL

[
92
]

As far as the incidental appeal of
Ms. Bruker is concerned to increase the damages awarded by the trial
judge, it follows that it must also be dismissed.

[
93
]

I therefore feel constrained to refrain from
commenting on the able arguments of counsel relating to the judgment of
Hacohen, J. of the Jerusalem Family Court in the case of
Jane Doe
v.

John Doe
in which extensive damages were awarded to a Jewish woman as the result
of the refusal of her former husband to give her a
ghet
, even after he
had been ordered to do so by a rabbinical court. I am all the more regretful
since, unfortunately for Ms. Bruker, she had to incur the expense of
paying for a certified translation of the judgment from Hebrew to English,
which was necessary if the members of the Court were going to be able to make
any sense of the judgment should it have been necessary to examine the
substance of the incidental appeal. In any event, the judgment would have been
of limited value inasmuch as matters of marriage and divorce of Jewish persons
are within the jurisdiction of religious tribunals in Israel, and the factual
context examined in the
Doe
case was very different from that which
obtains in this case.

[
94
]

For the same reason as I propose to allow
Mr. Marcovitz' appeal without costs, I would also deny costs to him on the
incidental appeal, however, an additional reason leads me to this conclusion
that is unrelated to the academic nature of the incidental appeal.

[
95
]

The second paragraph of article 26 of the
Rules
of Practice of the Court of Appeal in Civil

Matters
[53]

provides that an appellant in the
position of Mr. Marcovitz may, in reply to an incidental appeal such as
that of Ms. Bruker, "serve and file a factum in the form prescribed
for the factum of the respondent, within thirty days following receipt of the
factum of the incidental appellant". In this case, counsel for
Mr. Marcovitz filed her factum on the incidental appeal not 30 days,
but several months after her receipt of the factum of Ms. Bruker on the
incidental appeal, and also well after the time allotted for the hearing of the
appeal had been determined. As one might expect, the factum filed on behalf of
Mr. Marcovitz as incidental respondent was extremely detailed in light of
the conclusion in the incidental appeal that sought to increase the damages
awarded to $1,350,000.

[
96
]

Despite the non‑compliance with the clear
requirements of the foregoing provision of this Court's
Rules of Practice
,
my colleagues and I decided to accept the factum since it seems
Mr. Marcovitz' counsel had been misinformed by someone from the Court's
Registry as to when it could be filed. The misinformation apparently stemmed
from the belief that since the
Code of Civil Procedure
did not
specifically provide for an order of foreclosure such as is the case under
article 505
C.C.P
. when the respondent to an appeal fails to file
its factum on a timely basis, the time limit of thirty days was not peremptory
and therefore the factum of the incidental respondent could be filed without
reference to the delay provided for in the
Rules of Practice
.

[
97
]

My colleagues and I were then of the view, which
was communicated to both counsel, that although the time limit in the second
paragraph of article 26 of the
Rules of Practice
is not peremptory,
an incidental respondent who wished to file a factum beyond the thirty‑day
time limit would nevertheless require permission from the Court to do so. We
therefore took the written explanation of counsel explaining the reason for the
delay as if it was a motion and granted it, subject to a disposition as to
costs in the event the incidental appeal was dismissed.

[
98
]

Since the incidental appeal will be dismissed, I
believe the foregoing additional reason also warrants the dismissal without
costs as a sanction for the non‑compliance with the
Rules of Practice
,
in the same way that the Court invariably refuses to allow for the costs of
preparation of authorities when they are filed outside the thirty‑day
time limit contemplated by paragraph two of article 18 of the
Rules
of Practice
.

THE PUBLICATION BAN

[
99
]

In the conclusions of his judgment, the trial
judge included the following two paragraphs:

[60]
ORDERS
a publication
ban with respect to the names of the parties and their two children.

[61]
RECOMMENDS
that the
publication ban be respected beyond the jurisdiction of this Court.

[
100
]

His justification for doing so is found at the
beginning of his judgment in the following terms:

[2]    By judgment of March 16
th
,
2000, the Court imposed a publicity ban in this matter under the following
terms:

"RULING FOR THE MEDIAS

In view of some of the sensitive
issues which have come before the Court to this moment in this trial, and may
continue to come before the Court in this trial, any reports in the media
concerning any testimony adduced shall in no way identify either of the parties
or any of the witnesses, nor shall the contents and description of any of the
exhibits be reproduced or identified."

[3]    Inasmuch as the present
action derives originally from a family matter and involves evidence of a
highly personal nature, such as psychological and medical reports, children's
testimony, etc. and in virtue of Article 815.4 C.P.C., the court is of the
opinion that the aforesaid publicity ban should continue to remain in force
from the present date without any limitation of time and with the express hope
that such ban will be respected outside the Court's territorial jurisdiction.

[
101
]

It should be noted immediately that the trial
judge imposed the publication ban after seven days of trial had been completed,
and that the record does not disclose that any part of the trial took place
in
camera
.

[
102
]

In my opinion, the fact that the origin of this
civil case is a family law matter, and that the subjects under review involve
matters of a highly personal nature, including various medical and
psychological assessments as well as children's testimony, was insufficient in
law to justify a publication ban.
[54]
This is not a
family law case, but an action in damage for breach of contract.

[
103
]

As a matter of general application,
article 13
C.C.P.
and
section 23
of the
Quebec
Charter
of Human Rights and Freedoms
[55]

enshrine the principle that sittings of the courts are public and
may only be held
in camera
when issues of good order or morals are at
stake. As I have mentioned, the trial in this civil case proceeded in public,
which suggests that there were no reasons of good order or morals that would
have justified a hearing
in camera
.

[
104
]

Article 815.4
C.C.P.
, on which the
trial judge relied to issue the publication ban after the trial had begun and
which he reaffirmed for the future in his judgments, reads as follows:

No information that would allow the
identification of a party to a proceeding or of a child whose interest is at
stake in a proceeding may be published or broadcast unless the court or the law
authorizes it or unless that publication or broadcast is necessary to permit
the application of an Act or a regulation.

Furthermore, the judge may, in a
special case, prohibit or restrict, for such time and on such conditions as he
may deem fair and reasonable, the publication or broadcast of information
pertaining to a sitting of the court.

[
105
]

As this Court observed in
(D) J.L.
v.

Vallée
[56]
and
B.B.
v.

Procureur général du Québec et al.
,
[57]

a two‑step process should be followed before a court imposes a
publication ban. These steps are, first, to consider whether a publication ban
is necessary to avoid a compelling risk that a trial would be inequitable, and,
second, to consider whether the beneficial effects of the ban would outweigh
the prejudicial effects on the free expression of those who would be affected
by the ban.
[58]
A further condition is that an application to preserve anonymity
must be made
in limine litis
,

[59]

which, as I noted in paragraph [101], was not the case here.

[
106
]

The facts giving rise to the judgment in
Vallée
,
in which this Court, amongst other conclusions, did authorize a plaintiff to
use his initials instead of his name in any proceeding subsequent to the
declaration and ordered the non‑publication of any fact, element, exhibit
or proceeding in the Superior Court until a final judgment had been rendered in
a related criminal case in which the defendant was the accused, illustrates the
exceptional nature of publication bans.

[
107
]

The adult plaintiff in that case instituted a
civil action against a defendant who he alleged had sodomized him over a period
of 10 years while he was a minor. The applicant persuaded our Court that
there would be a serious breach of his fundamental rights in light of his
psychological state and the particular nature of the sexual abuse to which he
claimed to have been subjected.
[60]

[
108
]

No such comparable circumstances exist in this
case.

[
109
]

If anything, the circumstances of this case,
insofar as a publication ban is concerned, more closely resemble those
described in
B.R.
et
D.J.
v.
Létourneau Photographe inc
.
[61]

There, my colleague Dalphond, J.A., then a judge of the Superior Court, denied
an application in which the parties requested a publication ban, an
in camera

hearing and authorization to be designated in the proceedings only by their
initials. The plaintiffs were seeking an injunction and damages for the
allegedly unauthorized publication of intimate nude photographs they had taken
of them by the defendant at their request. While conceding that it was
undeniable that the photos were an aspect of their private lives that might
well be brought to the attention of persons who knew them, my colleague
concluded nevertheless that there was no basis in fact or in law to grant an
exception to the general rule of the public nature of legal proceedings.
[62]

[
110
]

I do not doubt that the revelation of the facts
and the arguments I have described in my reasons may well be a source of
embarrassment for the parties. That, however, is not enough to justify a
publication ban. The judicial reports are replete with cases that contain
information of a highly personal nature that are published nevertheless without
restriction. It should also be noted that very little of the judgment of the
Superior Court, and none of my reasons, make any reference to medical or
psychological factors, or mention anything about the children except in the
most peripheral way.

[
111
]

I therefore consider that whatever the
circumstances may have been when the trial was being conducted, there was no
valid reason in law to issue a publication ban. It will therefore be vacated,
as will the recommendation that followed it, which in any event was not
executory and thus had no compulsory effect on anyone.

DISPOSITION

[
112
]

In summary, I would allow the appeal, without
costs, and dismiss the respondent's action in the Superior Court, without
costs. I would also dismiss the respondent's incidental appeal, without costs.
The order of a publication ban with respect to the names of the parties and
their two children, as well as the recommendation that it be respected beyond
the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, will be vacated.
